title: The Rice Husk Plant in Tamkuha and the Villagers Who Paid for Light
dek: In August 2007 two engineers back from America lit a Bihar village with gas from mill waste, unsure anyone would pay for it.

story.founder: Gyanesh Pandey, Ratnesh Yadav, Manoj Sinha, Charles Ransler
story.event: Opening the first rice-husk power plant in Tamkuha, Bihar, and finding villagers would pay
story.summary: In August 2007 Gyanesh Pandey and Ratnesh Yadav opened a small power plant in Tamkuha, West Champaran, Bihar, that ran an engine on gas made from rice husk alone and sold villagers evening electricity. To the founders' surprise villagers paid, and on that evidence they and co-founders Manoj Sinha and Charles Ransler won business plan prizes, registered Husk Power Systems in 2008 and by March 2011 ran 65 plants serving about 32,500 households.
paragraphs: In August 2007 a small power plant was inaugurated in Tamkuha, a village in the West Champaran district of Bihar, one of India's worst-supplied states for electricity. People there travelled to town to charge their mobile phones, and by one later account the area had been notorious for kidnappings and robberies only a year or two before. The plant ran on rice husk, the papery waste of the local mills. Behind it were Gyanesh Pandey, an electrical engineer from a village in the same district who had worked in the semiconductor industry in Los Angeles, and his friend Ratnesh Yadav.

They had ruled out solar panels and wind as too costly; Manoj Sinha, who studied engineering with Pandey and would join as a co-founder, later put solar at about twenty times the price. What Bihar had in abundance was husk. Rice millers there had used gasifiers, which heat biomass with little air to make a burnable gas, for decades. With help from S. K. Singh, a government renewable-energy scientist, the team adapted the technology so an engine could run on husk gas alone rather than mixed with diesel, a hard problem because the gas carries tar. The first plant, of about 30 kilowatts, was set up through a foundation they had created for the purpose.

The open question was whether villagers would pay. Jacqueline Novogratz of the Acumen Fund, who visited early on, found people willing but wary of two city men from Patna. The founders strung up poles and wires and supplied power mostly in the evenings, for about 80 to 100 rupees a month for two compact fluorescent lamps and phone charging. "To our surprise, we were getting paid for the service we were providing," Sinha said later.

On that evidence the partners, now joined by Sinha and the American Charles Ransler, wrote a business plan. It won first place at the University of Virginia's 2008 competition among others, about $100,000 in prizes, which they put into Husk Power Systems, registered as a company in 2008. The Shell Foundation added $250,000. By the end of March 2011, the Ashden awards counted 65 working plants supplying about 32,500 households.

quote.text: But the truth is, that while the art of medicine gives health, and the art of the builder builds a house, another art attends them which is the art of pay.
quote.source_title: The Republic, tr. Benjamin Jowett, Project Gutenberg eBook #1497
quote.connection: Husk became a business on the evenings villagers handed over their fees, and the founders were surprised they would. Socrates insists the light and the fee are separate arts: one serves the villager, the other keeps the provider going. The story shows how much the second made the first possible; it does not show they cannot pull apart.

reflection: The founders learned something in Tamkuha that no survey could have told them: people with very little money would pay every month for light they could rely on. That payment turned an experiment into a company.

Plato would not let the two blur. Being paid tells you that something is wanted; it does not tell you that it is good, or that it is the best you could offer. At an early stage any payment can feel like proof. It is evidence, and a welcome kind. It is still worth asking, separately, what the work itself is doing for the person on the other end.
invitation: Think of one thing someone pays you for, in money, thanks or time. Write one sentence on what it does for them that has nothing to do with the payment.

sources.title: Husk Power Systems (Ashden Award winner, 2011)
sources.supports: Bihar's grid meets an estimated 10% of demand and most households use kerosene; the first plant running on 100% producer gas commissioned in 2007; Husk Power Systems registered as a for-profit company in 2008; founders Gyanesh Pandey, Ratnesh Yadav and Manoj Sinha from Bihar and Charles Ransler from the USA; Shell Foundation grants; engines developed to run on rice-husk gas alone rather than dual-fuel with diesel, a challenge because of tar; fees from INR 100 a month for two 15 W CFLs and phone charging; 65 operational plants and about 32,500 households by the end of March 2011.

sources.title: Husk Power (project disclosure)
sources.supports: Husk Power Systems founded in 2008; first community system inaugurated in August 2007 in Tamkuha, Bihar; promoted by first-generation entrepreneurs Gyanesh Pandey, Ratnesh Yadav, Manoj Sinha and Charles Ransler, who won several business plan competitions in the United States.

sources.title: After Bihar, rice husk power to light up TN, Bengal villages
sources.publisher: Bihar Prabha, carrying a Press Trust of India report (July 2010)
sources.supports: Beginning with Tamkuha in West Champaran, where villagers had travelled kilometres to charge their phones; Pandey, from Baithania village, left a semiconductor career in the US; founded with Ratnesh Yadav, Manoj Sinha and Charles W. Ransler; assisted by S. K. Singh of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, the team reworked biomass gasification long used by Bihar's rice millers; base price Rs 80 a month for two CFLs and phone charging.

sources.title: Illuminating villages
sources.supports: Pandey grew up in a West Champaran village, studied at IT-BHU and Rensselaer, and worked in the semiconductor industry in Los Angeles; with his friend Ratnesh Yadav he ruled out solar and wind as too costly; in 2007 the first plant was set up in Tamkuha through an NGO they created, the Samta Samriddhi Foundation; Husk Power Systems established a year later; first place at the 2008 University of Virginia Business Plan Competition; about Rs 100 a month basic charge.

sources.title: Husk brings electricity to power-hungry Indian villages
sources.supports: Tamkuha in 2005-06 known for kidnappings, looting and dacoity; in 2007 one of the first villages Husk lit; Sinha and Pandey studied engineering together at BHU; the small 30 kW experimental plant with wires and poles supplying power mostly at night; Sinha's quotation 'To our surprise, we were getting paid for the service we were providing'; business plan prizes of around $100,000 invested in the company; registered in 2008 with four founders; Shell Foundation $250,000 in 2008; by 2017 Sinha the only founder still running the company.

sources.title: 12000 Households, 350+ Villages: How Crop Waste is Electrifying Rural India!
sources.supports: Manoj Sinha's account: solar explored first and found about 20 times more expensive; initial 30 kW biomass gasification unit for about 300 families; power only at night at first; business plan prizes of around $100,000 invested in the company; initial capital of about Rs 50 lakh for two plants.

sources.title: Roshan Tara Lights the World
sources.supports: Tamkuha as the site of Husk's first gasifier plant; on her first visit, when the company had just started, villagers were willing but wary of depending on Gyanesh and Ratnesh, two city men from Patna; later evening businesses and study by electric light.

sources.title: Electrifying India with rice husk
sources.supports: Pandey, from Baithania village, and his friend Ratnesh Yadav founded Husk Power Systems in 2007; pre-paid billing of about Rs 80 a month for two CFLs and phone charging; about 270 staff in 2010; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy subsidy extended to fit the project.

cross_checks.claim: Husk's first plant was inaugurated in Tamkuha, Bihar, in 2007 (August, per the IFC).
The founders ruled out solar as too expensive and chose rice-husk gasification.
The plant ran an engine on rice-husk gas alone, adapted from gasifiers used by rice millers, with help from a ministry scientist.
The first plant was about 30 kW and supplied power mainly in the evenings.
Villagers paid about 80 to 100 rupees a month for two CFLs and phone charging.
Business plan prizes of about $100,000 were invested and the company was registered in 2008.
The plan won the University of Virginia business plan competition in 2008, among others.

research_notes: Founders and credit: the 2010 accounts (Business Standard, PTI) and The Weekend Leader present the Tamkuha plant as the work of Pandey and his friend Ratnesh Yadav; later accounts given by Manoj Sinha (Business Standard 2017, The Better India 2018, JSTOR Daily) describe the first experiment as his and Pandey's; Ashden and the IFC list four founders. The story credits Pandey and Yadav with the 2007 plant and has Sinha and Ransler joining as co-founders for the 2008 company, while quoting Sinha's later account of being paid. Pandey's US work: The Weekend Leader and PTI say he worked in (and left) the semiconductor industry in Los Angeles/the US; Business Standard (2010) says he 'rejected an opportunity' to work there; the story follows the two that agree. Date: the IFC gives August 2007 for Tamkuha; Ashden and others give 2007; a BusinessWorld listing seen in search gives 2008 and is not used. The first plant was set up through the Samta Samriddhi Foundation (The Weekend Leader) before the company was registered in 2008, so funding is 'mixed': founders' money and an NGO at first, then prize money, Shell Foundation grants ($250,000 in 2008), social-investor equity and Ministry of New and Renewable Energy capital subsidies. Prices: Rs 80 a month (PTI and Business Standard 2010) and Rs 100 (Ashden, The Weekend Leader); the story says 80 to 100 rupees. Investment figures differ: Ashden says $1.65 million from six investors in December 2009; Business Standard (2017) says $1.56 million in 2010; not used. Scale figures differ by date and source (125+ villages, PTI July 2010; 200 villages, Business Standard September 2010; 80 plants and 350 villages, The Weekend Leader June 2011; 65 operational plants and about 32,500 households by March 2011, Ashden); the story uses Ashden's dated plant and household count, since 'villages' is counted differently by each source. Better India puts the first unit at about 300 families while Ashden gives about 500 customers per plant later; neither figure is used for Tamkuha. Sinha's quotation is in English in the source. Novogratz's Acumen Fund later invested in Husk; her piece is cited only for her first impressions of Tamkuha. The Plato passage is Socrates arguing with Thrasymachus about crafts and wages; it is applied to a company by analogy.
